title: A web-based cross-sectional observational study on the analysis of information on diabetes on a social media platform (Instagram)
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 600 top-performing Instagram posts under six diabetes hashtags; 448 relevant posts were each coded for the authenticity of their information against the latest WHO guidelines on diabetes, giving a share of items classified false (19/448, 4.24%). That is a CONTENT prevalence share with a denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated (Instagram hashtag posts in English or Hindi; authors based in India)
estimates.measure_type: % of diabetes-related Instagram posts whose information was judged false (misinformation) against WHO diabetes guidelines
estimates.denominator: 448 posts judged relevant to diabetes, out of the 600 top-performing posts collected (top 100 under each of six diabetes hashtags)
estimates.definition: A post was coded 'False' when its information was not authentic/verified according to the latest WHO guidelines on diabetes; 'True' (208, 46.43%) and 'Cannot be determined' (221, 49.33%) were the other two categories
estimates.misinfo_def: Source of information (true or false) according to the latest WHO guidelines on diabetes
estimates.source_quote: The authenticity of the information presented via the published posts was unable to be determined in 221 posts (49.33%). Authentic and verified information was published in 208 posts (46.43%) and misinformation was reported in 19 posts (4.24%). (Table 8)
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 66; Table 8 'Authenticity of information in the published posts (N = 448)'; Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four researchers each took one or two hashtags, collected the post data via Google Forms and rated each post's information as true or false against the latest WHO guidelines on diabetes; uncertainties were discussed with a mentor; no inter-rater reliability statistic and no double-coding reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The study was conducted among the top-performing hundred posts tagged under each of the six hashtags, making a total of 600 posts. ... 6. Source of information (true or false) according to the latest WHO guidelines on diabetes
estimates.notes: Denominator is the 448 relevant posts, not the 600 collected. Because authenticity 'could not be determined' for 49.33% of posts, 4.24% is a floor on falsity within this corpus. Rank-truncated (top-performing) hashtag sample, hence denom_selection=curated. Country is not restricted by the study (global Instagram, posts in English or Hindi kept); coded Global rather than India. Unrelated typos elsewhere in the paper (94.64% vs 96.64% images; 39.26% vs 39.29% 'others'; a mangled '810.71%' table cell) do not touch this cell: 19/448 = 4.24%.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: the 46.43% 'true' and 49.33% 'cannot be determined' cells (not misinformation shares); source-of-post shares (39.29% unverified sources such as bloggers/patients/influencers) because these code who posted, not whether the content is false; the engagement, duration, language and information-completeness tables (e.g. 92.19% gave no prevalence information) are completeness/quality, not falsity.

rob.design: Web-based cross-sectional content analysis; sampling frame = the top-performing 100 posts under each of the 6 most-searched diabetes hashtags (600 posts, 448 relevant) collected in one week (third week of August 2022); four researchers split the hashtags and coded via Google Forms, no double-coding, no kappa reported; disagreements/uncertainty resolved with a mentor.
rob.item6_quote: 6. Source of information (true or false) according to the latest WHO guidelines on diabetes
rob.item10_quote: Authentic and verified information was published in 208 posts (46.43%) and misinformation was reported in 19 posts (4.24%).
